nota.t: 1.1 Integers

Integers ialah nombor bulat positif, sifar dan nombor bulat negatif. Nombor negatif menunjukkan arah atau keadaan yang bertentangan, contohnya suhu di bawah 0 °C atau kedalaman di bawah aras laut. Pada garis nombor, nombor di sebelah kanan sentiasa lebih besar.
Integers are positive whole numbers, negative whole numbers and zero: …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …

t: Negative numbers show the opposite direction: below sea level, temperatures below zero, debt.
On a number line, the number on the right is always greater.
−2 > −9 because −2 is further right.

nota.t: 1.2 Basic operations on integers

Adding integers with the same sign: add the values and keep the sign. Different signs: subtract the smaller value from the larger and take the sign of the larger. Multiplying or dividing: same signs give a positive, different signs give a negative. Order: brackets, multiply/divide, then add/subtract.

baris: Same signs: add. Different: subtract, take the sign of the bigger number

nota.t: Order of operations: brackets → multiply and divide (left to right) → add and subtract (left to right).

t: Commutative: a + b = b + a, a × b = b × a
Associative: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c)
Distributive: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c
Identity: a + 0 = a, a × 1 = a

nota.t: Common mistake: thinking −8 is greater than −3. The further left, the smaller.
1.3 Positive and negative fractions

Negative fractions lie to the left of zero. To add or subtract fractions, make the denominators the same first; to multiply, multiply numerators and denominators; to divide, multiply by the reciprocal. The integer sign rules still apply.
Use a common denominator to add and subtract. To divide, multiply by the reciprocal. Signs follow the integer rules.
1.4 Positive and negative decimals
Negative decimals such as −0.5 lie between −1 and 0. Work as with integers, then place the decimal point: when multiplying, the answer has as many decimal places as the numbers together.

v.c: Positive and negative decimals on a number line

nota.t: Work it out with whole numbers, then put in the decimal point (decimal places in a product = the total decimal places of both numbers).
1.5 Rational numbers

A rational number can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Integers, fractions and decimals (terminating or repeating) are all rational numbers. Mixed operations follow the order of operations.

v.c: All of these are rational numbers

nota.t: Rational numbers can be written in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Integers, fractions, and terminating or recurring decimals are rational numbers.
π and √2 are not rational numbers: their decimals neither end nor repeat.
2.1 Factors, prime factors and HCF

A factor divides a number exactly with no remainder. A prime number has only two factors: 1 and itself. The highest common factor (HCF) is the largest factor shared by two or more numbers, found by prime factorisation or repeated division.
A factor of a number divides it exactly with no remainder. A prime number has only two factors: 1 and itself.
Prime factorisation: write the number as a product of prime factors, e.g. 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
HCF (highest common factor): multiply the common prime factors.
2.2 Multiples and LCM

A multiple is a number times 1, 2, 3, … A common multiple is shared; the lowest common multiple (LCM) is the smallest one. The LCM helps to make denominators the same and to solve problems such as when two schedules meet again.
LCM (lowest common multiple): the smallest multiple they share. With prime factors: take each factor with its highest power.
'Share equally, as many as possible' problems → HCF. 'When do they meet / happen together again' problems → LCM.

topik.nama: 3. Squares, Square Roots, Cubes and Cube Roots

nota.t: 3.1 Squares and square roots
The square of a number is the number multiplied by itself, e.g. 5² = 25, the area of a square of side 5. The square root is the inverse: √25 = 5. Perfect squares are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …
Estimate: √50 is between 7 (49) and 8 (64), closer to 7.
3.2 Cubes and cube roots

A cube is a number multiplied by itself three times, e.g. 3³ = 27, the volume of a cube of side 3. The cube root is the inverse: ∛27 = 3. The cube root of a negative number is negative, e.g. ∛(−8) = −2.
a³ = a × a × a. ∛(a³) = a. Negative numbers: (−3)³ = −27, ∛(−27) = −3.
Common mistake: writing (−4)² = −16. In fact (−4)² = 16, but −4² = −16.
4.1 Ratios

A ratio compares two or more quantities with the same unit, written a : b. Equivalent ratios come from multiplying or dividing every part by the same number, e.g. 2 : 3 = 4 : 6. Ratios are written in lowest terms.
A ratio compares two or more quantities in the same unit: a : b. Simplify by dividing by the HCF.
4.2 Rates
A rate compares two quantities with different units, such as speed (km/h), price (RM/kg) or pulse rate (beats/minute). A unit rate makes comparison easy: divide the first quantity by the second.

v.c: Rate 60 km/h: distance grows 60 km each hour

nota.t: A rate compares two quantities with different units: km/h, RM/kg, litres/minute. Speed = distance ÷ time.
1 km/h = 1 000 m ÷ 3 600 s. km/h → m/s: multiply by 5/18. m/s → km/h: multiply by 18/5.
4.3 Proportions
A proportion states that two ratios are equal: a/b = c/d. An unknown value is found by cross-multiplying (a × d = b × c) or the unitary method, finding the value of one unit first.
Proportion: two equal ratios, a : b = c : d. Solve by cross-multiplying (a × d = b × c) or by the unitary method.
4.4 Ratios, rates and proportions
Ratio, rate and proportion problems are solved by identifying the quantities compared, writing the ratio or rate, then using proportion. Example: if 3 books cost RM12, then 5 books cost RM20.
Sharing a quantity in a ratio: find one part (total ÷ total number of parts), then multiply.
Inverse proportion: more workers → less time. The product stays the same, not the ratio.
5.1 Variables and algebraic expressions

A variable is a letter standing for an unknown or changing value, such as x. An algebraic expression combines numbers, variables and operations, like 3x + 2. Like terms have the same variables and powers.
A variable is a letter that stands for an unknown value. An algebraic term: number × variable, e.g. 5x, −3ab. Coefficient: the number in front of the variable.
Like terms have the same variables with the same powers: 2xy and −7yx are like terms; 2x and 2x² are not.
5.2 Operations on algebraic expressions

Only like terms can be added or subtracted: 4a + 3a = 7a, but 4a + 3b stays. When multiplying, multiply coefficients and variables: 2a × 3b = 6ab. When dividing, simplify like a fraction: 6ab ÷ 2a = 3b.

t: Add/subtract: combine like terms only.
Multiply: multiply the coefficients, then the variables (x × x = x²).
Divide: write it as a fraction and simplify.
Expand: a(b + c) = ab + ac.

nota.t: Common mistake: 3x + 2y = 5xy. Unlike terms cannot be combined.
6.1 Linear equations in one variable
A linear equation in one variable has highest power 1, e.g. 2x + 3 = 11. Solve by doing the same operation to both sides so the equation stays balanced: subtract 3, then divide by 2, so x = 4.

v.c: An equation as a balance: x = 4

nota.t: A linear equation has an = sign and variables to the power 1. Solve it by doing the same operation on both sides.
6.2 Linear equations in two variables
A linear equation in two variables, such as x + y = 5, has many solutions (x, y). Each pair of values that satisfies it is a point, and all the points form a straight line when plotted.

v.c: Solutions of x + y = 4 lie on a line

nota.t: For example, 2x + y = 10 has many solutions (x, y): (0, 10), (3, 4), (5, 0)… Its graph is a straight line.
6.3 Simultaneous linear equations

Simultaneous linear equations are two equations with the same two variables. The solution is the pair of values that satisfies both, found by substitution, elimination or where the two straight lines cross.

v.c: Two lines meet at the solution (3, 1)

t: Substitution: write one variable in terms of the other, then substitute it into the second equation.
Elimination: make the coefficients of one variable equal, then add or subtract the equations.
Graph: the point where the two lines cross is the solution.

nota.t: Always check the answer by substituting it into both equations.
7.1 Inequalities
An inequality compares two unequal values using <, >, ≤ or ≥. On a number line, an open circle means the value is not included (< or >) and a filled circle means it is included (≤ or ≥).

t: Add/subtract the same number: the symbol stays.
Multiply/divide by a positive number: the symbol stays.
Multiply/divide by a negative number: the symbol reverses.

nota.t: 7.2 Linear inequalities in one variable
A linear inequality such as 2x − 1 > 5 is solved like an equation: x > 3. But if both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number, the inequality sign must be reversed.
3 − 2x > 9 → −2x > 6 → x < −3 (divide by −2, the symbol reverses)
Simultaneous inequalities: find the values that satisfy both inequalities, e.g. x > −1 and x ≤ 3 → −1 < x ≤ 3.
The most common mistake: forgetting to reverse the symbol when dividing by a negative number.
8.1 Lines and angles

A line has no ends; a line segment has two ends. Angles are measured in degrees: acute (< 90°), right (90°), obtuse (90°–180°), straight (180°) and reflex (> 180°). Complementary angles add up to 90°, supplementary angles to 180°.

t: Complementary: two angles that add up to 90°.
Supplementary: two angles that add up to 180°.
Conjugate: two angles that add up to 360°.
Angles at a point add up to 360°; on a straight line, 180°.

nota.t: 8.2 Intersecting lines
When two lines intersect, vertically opposite angles are equal, and adjacent angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Angles around a point add up to 360°.
When two lines intersect, vertically opposite angles are equal, and adjacent angles add up to 180°.
8.3 Parallel lines and transversals
A transversal crossing two parallel lines makes corresponding angles (equal), alternate angles (equal) and interior angles (adding to 180°). These are used to find unknown angles.

t: Corresponding angles (F shape) are equal.
Alternate angles (Z shape) are equal.
Interior angles (C/U shape) add up to 180°.

nota.t: Mark the arrows on the parallel lines first, then look for an F, Z or C shape in the diagram.
9.1 Polygons

A polygon is a closed shape made of straight line segments. Polygons are named by their number of sides: triangle (3), quadrilateral (4), pentagon (5), hexagon (6), heptagon (7), octagon (8). A diagonal joins two non-adjacent vertices.
A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides. Number of diagonals = n(n − 3) ÷ 2.
9.2 Triangles

The interior angles of a triangle add up to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. Triangles are classified by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles (acute, right, obtuse).

t: The interior angles add up to 180°.
Exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles.
Isosceles triangle: two equal sides and two equal base angles.
Equilateral triangle: every angle is 60°.

nota.t: 9.3 Quadrilaterals

The interior angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°. Special quadrilaterals include the square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, trapezium and kite, each with its own properties of sides, angles and diagonals.

baris: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles, diagonals equal & perpendicular
opposite sides equal, 4 right angles, diagonals equal
opposite sides equal & parallel, opposite angles equal
2 pairs of equal adjacent sides, diagonals perpendicular

nota.t: The interior angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°.
10.1 Perimeter
Perimeter is the total length around a shape. For a composite shape, add only the outside edges. The perimeter of a rectangle = 2(length + width).
Perimeter = the total length of all the sides around the outside of a shape.
10.2 Area
Area measures a surface in square units. Triangle: ½ × base × height. Parallelogram: base × height. Trapezium: ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height. Kite: ½ × product of diagonals.

baris: ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × height

nota.t: The height is always perpendicular to the base, not along the slanted side.
10.3 Perimeter and area
Shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas, and the other way round. For a fixed perimeter, a square gives the largest rectangle area.

v.c: Perimeter 20: a 5 × 5 square gives the largest area, 25

nota.t: Shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas. For a fixed perimeter, a square gives the largest area of all rectangles.
11.1 Sets

A set is a well-defined collection of objects; each object is an element, written with ∈. Sets are described in words, set notation { } or a Venn diagram. n(A) is the number of elements of A; the empty set is { } or ∅.

v.c: Set A in a Venn diagram

nota.t: A set is a collection of objects with a common feature. Each object is an element (∈). n(A) = the number of elements. The empty set ∅ or { } has no elements.

t: Description: A = {prime numbers less than 10}
Set notation: A = {2, 3, 5, 7}
Equal sets: the same elements, order does not matter

nota.t: 11.2 Venn diagrams, universal set, complement and subsets
The universal set ξ contains all the elements being discussed. The complement A′ is the elements of ξ not in A. B is a subset of A (B ⊂ A) if every element of B is also in A.

v.c: B is a subset of A

t: Universal set ξ: all the elements being discussed (the rectangle).
Complement A′: the elements of ξ not in A.
Subset B ⊂ A: every element of B is in A. A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets.

nota.t: Common mistake: thinking {0} is the empty set. It has one element, 0.
12.1 Collecting, classifying and representing data

Handling data has four steps: collecting (surveys, interviews, observation), organising (frequency tables), representing (bar charts, pie charts, pictographs, line graphs, stem-and-leaf plots) and interpreting to draw conclusions.

t: Categorical data: labels (colour, brand).
Discrete numerical data: counted (number of pupils).
Continuous numerical data: measured (height, time).

nota.t: Sector angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360°
12.2 Interpreting data

The statistical investigation cycle starts with a question, then collecting, organising and representing data, and interpreting the results to answer the question. The cycle repeats if a new question comes up.
Read the scale carefully, compare, draw conclusions and make predictions. Watch out for misleading graphs: a scale that does not start at 0, unequal intervals, or icons of different sizes.
13.1 Pythagoras' theorem

Pythagoras' theorem: in a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, c² = a² + b². The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle.
In a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse c: c² = a² + b².

t: To find the hypotenuse: c = √(a² + b²)
To find another side: a = √(c² − b²)

nota.t: Pythagorean triples: (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25) and their multiples
13.2 Converse of Pythagoras' theorem
The converse: if c² = a² + b² for the sides of a triangle, the triangle is right-angled. If c² < a² + b² the angle opposite c is acute; if c² > a² + b² it is obtuse.
If c² = a² + b² for the longest side c, the triangle is right-angled. If c² > a² + b², the angle opposite c is obtuse; if c² < a² + b², it is acute.
Make sure c is the longest side before using the formula.
